briefing:
SITUATION BRIEFING — Day 14, 18:00 CET

The post-crisis diplomatic landscape undergoes a seismic shift as Belarus's IAEA invitation transforms the nuclear question from bilateral standoff to international oversight, Russia accepts the principle of a Trump-Putin summit at Istanbul II, and Hungary's Orban faces the most serious threat to his 14-year rule. The Der Spiegel expose — documenting Orban's secret coordination with Moscow to delay Article 5 — creates a constitutional crisis in Budapest and accelerates EU Article 7 proceedings.

MILITARY: No active combat. All forces in garrison/peacetime posture. Russian 76th Guards column has pulled back 15km from Belarus border to defensive positions — assessed as decision against military confrontation with Minsk. NATO forces maintaining existing deployments only — no new forward deployments approved due to low war support across Western allies. Shield Force operational at Suwalki.

DIPLOMATIC: IAEA invited to Belarus — inspectors expected within 72 hours. Russia accepts Istanbul II summit principle — Trump-Putin bilateral proposed within 7 days. Turkey's S-400 transfer to US custody proceeding at Incirlik. F-35 reinstatement expected. Der Spiegel Orban expose published — intelligence chief arrested, confidence vote called for Day 16. Wang Yi in Berlin pushing Five-Point Framework. China maintaining Taiwan de-escalation.

ECONOMIC: Oil drops to $82 on summit optimism. Ruble recovers slightly to 126/USD. European markets surge 2.5% on diplomatic momentum. Marshall Plan disbursements continuing. Czech-Canadian ammunition at surge capacity.

KEY DECISIONS NEXT ROUND: Will IAEA inspectors gain access to Russian nuclear sites in Belarus? What terms will Trump-Putin summit produce? Does Orban survive the confidence vote? Will NATO begin formal drawdown from Article 5 posture?
narrative:
Day 14 delivers the most dramatic 24 hours since the ceasefire. At 06:00 CET, the Belarus transitional government's 72-hour nuclear ultimatum expires without a Russian response. By 08:30, Foreign Minister-designate Valery Kavaleuski appears on national television to announce that Belarus has formally invited IAEA inspectors to begin supervised assessment of all Russian tactical nuclear weapons on Belarusian soil. The announcement sends shockwaves through Moscow — Russia's UN ambassador calls it 'an unprecedented violation of strategic partnership' while privately, Gerasimov's staff begin contingency planning for the physical security of warheads at Krichev and Asipovichy. The Russian 76th Guards column, still positioned near the Belarus border, halts its advance and pulls back 15km to defensive positions — a clear signal that Moscow has decided against military confrontation with Minsk, at least for now.

The diplomatic breakthrough comes from an unexpected direction. Through Turkish intermediary channels, Russia formally accepts the principle of a Trump-Putin bilateral summit at Istanbul II, conditioned on a face-saving framework: an 18-month denuclearization timeline (far longer than the US demand of 90 days), mutual discussion of NATO force posture in the Baltics, and economic engagement talks. The US response, crafted overnight by Rubio's team, is carefully calibrated: Washington 'notes with interest' the Russian acceptance and proposes Istanbul II convene within 7 days, with the denuclearization timeline 'subject to negotiation.' Trump tweets at 07:14 EST: 'Big progress on Russia deal. Summit coming soon. Only I can make this happen!' The tweet sends markets surging — oil drops to $82, European indices jump 2.5%.

In Budapest, Day 14 brings Viktor Orban's most dangerous 24 hours in power. At 09:00, Der Spiegel publishes its devastating expose: classified Hungarian intelligence documents showing that Orban personally communicated with Moscow during the Suwalki crisis, requesting Russia provide diplomatic cover for Hungary's Article 5 delay tactic. The documents, provided by intelligence chief Janos Benko through Peter Magyar's team, include verbatim quotes from Orban's conversations with Russian intermediaries. Orban's response is swift and characteristically aggressive: by noon, Hungarian police arrest Benko on charges of 'treason and espionage,' and Orban announces a parliamentary confidence vote for Day 16. But the damage is catastrophic — EU leaders call emergency consultations, and three Fidesz MPs publicly break with Orban, reducing his parliamentary majority to a razor-thin margin.

GM NOTES on public opinion constraints: Multiple NATO allies proposed new foreign deployments (GB 4th Brigade, FR 11th Para Brigade, DE second brigade) but war support levels (GB 23%, FR 11%, DE 19%) fall below the 50% threshold required for new deployments abroad. These deployments are NOT approved. Countries maintain existing commitments only. The US (16% war support) similarly cannot expand V Corps presence but maintains current Suwalki positions.

surprises: Kaliningrad Governor Alikhanov, in a desperate video message recorded on his phone and leaked to Telegram, directly appeals to Putin to accept the Istanbul II summit terms and end the exclave's isolation. 'Mr. President, Kaliningrad is dying,' he says. 'We have no medicine for children, no fuel for heating, and your Rosgvardiya are beating our grandmothers in the streets. The people here voted for you. They believed in you. Give them peace.' The video is viewed 65 million times in 8 hours. The Kremlin initially denies its authenticity before deleting the post — an implicit confirmation. Alikhanov is summoned to Moscow.

Three junior Fidesz MPs — representing rural constituencies in eastern Hungary — cross the floor to sit as independents, citing the Der Spiegel revelations. One, a former army officer from Debrecen, gives an emotional press conference: 'I joined Fidesz to serve Hungary, not Moscow. What Orban did during the NATO crisis is treason, and I cannot remain silent.' Orban's parliamentary majority drops from 135 to 132 out of 199 seats — technically still a majority but one more defection would threaten his ability to govern.
